newsitem.title: UK: Two easy tests can discover E coli - magazine.
newsitem.headline: Two easy tests can discover E coli - magazine.

text.p: Scientists have developed two simple tests to detect the poisonous E coli strain of bacteria that can kill children and the elderly, New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.
One test involves something similar to litmus paper, while another uses magnets.
Ray Stevens and colleagues at the University of California at Berkeley said their test could be incorporated into meat packaging that would turn red if food was contaminated.

The test uses films of polymers, a common type of chained molecule, that mimic the surface membranes of human cells. Toxins produced by the E coli bacteria bind to the polymers as they would to human gut cells.
"When this happens, the polymer film kinks so that red light is reflected," Stevens told the weekly magazine.
"All the basic research has been done, and what we really need now is for a company to pick it up and turn it into a commercial product," he added.
"This stuff is so cheap, you could develop hundreds of litmus sensors for pennies."

A second test, developed by Prabhakara Choudary and Chris Gooding at the University of California at Davis, uses magnetic beads coated with antibodies that bind to the genes that produce E coli's toxins. Magnets draw the bead out of the sample.

E coli is a bacteria normally found in the guts of cattle, sheep and people. It is usually harmless but one strain, known as 0157, can cause brain damage and kidney failure in vulnerable people such as the elderly or children.
It gets into food via improper slaughtering techniques or through manure used as fertiliser.

In the latest outbreak, 15 people in Scotland have died and more than 300 have reported symptoms. The deadliest outbreak of E coli was in Canada, where 19 old people infected in a nursing home died in September 1985.
